Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to the SBFC Finance Limited Q2 FY '27 Earnings 
Conference Call. As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and there 
will be an opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. Should you need

Gaurav Toshniwal: 
Yes. Thank you, Steve. Hi. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to SBFC Finance Q2 FY '27 
Earnings Call. On behalf of ICICI Securities, I would like to thank SBFC management team for 
giving us the opportunity to host this call. Today, we have with us the entire top management 
team of SBFC, represented by Mr. Aseem Dhru, Executive Vice Chairman; Mr. Mahesh Dayani, 
MD & CEO; Mr. Sanket Agrawal, Chief Financial Officer; and Mr. Rajiv Thakker, Chief Risk 
Officer. I will now hand over the call to Aseem for his opening remarks, and then we'll open the 
floor for Q&A. Over to you, sir. 
Aseem Dhru: 
Thank you, Gaurav. Good morning, everyone. The world as we always knew it is in a kind of a 
reset. Geopolitics, geoeconomics, deglobalization, anti-immigration, and breakdown of a rules-
based order that we have been used to. In addition, it is readjusting to the changes AI is bringing 
into everything and every domain of life. Volatility and disruption are the new normals. In India, 
the impact of the 3F's – fuel, fertilizer and foreign exchange on top of a super El Nino is 
juxtaposed with a resilient domestic demand. 
 
There are 10 major schools of economic thought in the world; classical, neoclassical, Keynesian, 
Austrian, Marxism, etcetera. But what we are seeing defies all things we have been taught. The 
Fed trying to force the 10-year down, when it succeeds even temporarily, even gold and Bitcoin 
both go down, which could basically mean it's a risk-off. 
 
The U.S. 10-year crossing 5%, any economic theory would tell you, would lead to a stock market 
crash, but that is not what we are seeing. Honestly, it's getting increasingly difficult to make 
sense of the macroeconomic reality of the world we live in. As we speak, economic cycles, 
political cycles, commodity cycles, currency, interest rate cycles, liquidity cycles are in motion. 
 
And these usually lead to an eventual credit cycle. However, the causal relationships we have 
been taught in economic textbooks no longer work in a world where deficits and currency 
printing has gone out of control. Frankly, and thankfully, for a company as small as SBFC, these 
questions are above our pay grade. We have to manage to keep our little boat safe in this 
tempestuous ocean. If you listen to the last 3 years of quarterly calls, we have always been 
cautious and continue to remain so. Take for example, interest rates, 10-year Indian G-Sec at 
7.47% is up almost 65 basis points in this cycle and so surely, more rate hikes are coming. 
 
These aren't controllable for us. How we manage our borrowing cost and reprice our variable 
rate portfolio of loans is in our hands, and we will focus on the controllable. We don't have to 
worry so much about the health of the economy at our size. We just need to worry about choosing 
our customers better, using technology better, becoming more efficient producers – enabling us 
to deliver the ROAs, squeezing the opex and credit costs. In a world of constant flux and chaos, 
we are trying our best to continue to deliver boring results.

Mahesh Dayani: 
Thank you, Aseem. Good morning to all. There is never a dull moment in financial services. We 
began the year with a war that fueled inflation, and we ended up with a 25 basis rate increase. 
We are now debating the possibility of further rate increases, dealing with a deficient rainfall, 
watching cross-leverage buildup in gold loans, and assessing a draft regulatory circular that may 
impact profitability. The last couple of years have felt like a Bollywood thriller. There are 
moments when your heart is in your mouth, the background music gets louder and you wonder 
what the next twist will be. 
 
But once the dust settles, you find yourself relishing the drama. We are building SBFC to deliver 
consistent quarterly performance despite the noise. This is our 36th consecutive quarter of 
execution since inception, and we have delivered sequential AUM and profit growth within our 
guided range of 5% to 7% per quarter. It may not make for an exciting headline, but in lending, 
consistency is a competitive advantage. What made this quarter special was the 15% ROE on a 
low leverage of 2.3 while recognizing costs upfront and not front-loading income. For years, 
this number sat in a cell in our Excel model. It is satisfying to see an aspiration translate into a 
reported performance. Let me now return to the 3 priorities we outlined last quarter – growth, 
margins & efficiency, and asset quality.  
On growth: we are witnessing an interesting shift in the lending landscape. With a more cautious 
approach to risk, private and public sector banks are increasingly moving towards higher ticket 
prime borrowers where the credit profile is significantly stronger and pricing is in single digits. 
Needless to add, there's very little blood on the report card. The micro MSMEs category, which 
is a sub INR 7 lakh category has seen some stains on the progress report, with delinquencies 
touching more than 4% for the industry. This creates a meaningful headroom in the INR 10 lakh 
to INR 25 lakh and a INR 25+ lakh segment, which is where we have repositioned our business 
through our own book and co-lending. A direct co-origination model is like a large ship – it does 
not turn overnight, but once it changes direction the momentum can be substantial. The change 
is to make the turn early enough and stay the course long enough to see the benefits. MSME 
disbursements grew 6% in the quarter to INR 855 crores. This is the third straight quarter of 
growth since we repositioned our lending mix in quarter 2 last year. You cannot reliably predict 
every turn in the cycle, but you can prepare your business to respond to it. This is precisely what 
we have tried to do. MSME stood at INR 9,669 crores, growing at 18%, of which the on-book 
grew at 20% and the co-origination at 10%. We have repositioned our lending mix, strengthened 
our focus on secured MSME customers, and are now seeing the early benefits of that transition. 
Co-origination has returned to INR 112 crores from INR 78 crores last quarter. This supports 
our growth ambition, even as the sub INR 7 lakh segment continues to run down.  
Gold loans have held up well. Each branch is adding approximately INR 40 lakhs a month in 
net growth, that's roughly INR 1.2 crores per branch per quarter. We added overall INR 275 
crores in quarter 2. Gold has survived wars, inflation, currency crisis, and several financial 
cycles. Its resilience is one reason it remains an important asset class, but resilience should not 
be mistaken for immunity. We respect the product, understand its risks, and have no intention 
of over-leveraging it.

Overall, our AUM stood at INR 12,592 crores, up 6% Q-o-Q and 27% Y-o-Y. We continue to 
guide for a 5% to 7% growth on a quarterly basis from here on. Our approach to growth is 
straightforward – we want to grow where we have an edge, in segments where the risk-adjusted 
returns make sense, and at a pace our balance sheet can comfortably support.  
Margins and efficiency: Yields held up at 18%, up 10 basis points, while our cost of funds stood 
at 8.41%. We maintained surplus liquidity of more than INR 1,000 crores through the quarter, 
thanks in part to the work of our CFO, Sanket. I would encourage you to question him hard on 
the details. Spreads came in at 9.6%, up from 9.4% last quarter and above our guided range of 
9%. While this is a welcome outcome, please do not pencil in 9.6% in your models as the new 
norm, since competitive intensity in gold is rising and some pricing rationalization is likely. 
There is useful distinction between a number that looks good today and an economics model 
that continues to work tomorrow, we would rather preserve the latter.  
On operating efficiency, before we get into numbers, let me spend a minute on how SBFC runs 
today because it is the foundation under everything else you will hear this morning. Our 
customer journey is digital by default and compliant by construction. In September, 100% of 
our customer KYCs were completed digitally, Aadhaar OTP or face authentication, and 87% of 
our disbursements were e-signed. Account aggregator was at 54%, all built into Sahayak, our 
in-house origination platform. I want you to register what that means. Governance, compliance, 
and efficiency are no longer 3 functions we run in parallel, they are one outcome on the same 
platform. In September, 73% of our disbursements used AI-assisted personal discussions. 4,000 
AI personal discussions in 8 languages. So a credit officer, whether he's in Hapur or one in 
Yelahanka, are working from the same quality of conversation. 
 
In October, our first full pre-due collection cycle was run entirely by AI voice. More than 4 lakh 
calls made to 35,000 accounts, 84% reached, 53% paid with no human caller absorbing the 
workload of roughly a 60-person team. So when you look at the numbers that follow, I would 
ask you to see them for what they are, not growth that technology made possible, but growth 
that technology made safe. Opex declined to 4.07%, down 22 bps Q-o-Q. On a half year basis, 
it was 30 basis points lower Y-o-Y. We continue to guide for a 25 basis reduction in Opex for 
FY '27. The objective is not to become the cheapest operator in the market, it is to become a 
more efficient operator without compromising the quality of our franchise.  
Last quarter, I described the increase in 0+ delinquencies as our homework. This quarter, the 
position has stabilized, and credit cost declined to 1.37% from 1.44%. We have also been 
deliberate in provisioning through the transition away from the micro MSME lending, building 
a provision of 2%, which is the highest in secured lending. Our preference is to make sure that 
we are properly equipped before the tide turns. We bought the umbrella while the sun was 
shining so that if a difficult winter arrives, we are prepared. 
 
Coming to what really matters, PAT. We ended PAT at INR 139 crores for the quarter, up 7% 
Q-o-Q and 27% Y-o-Y. ROA stood at 4.6% and ROE at 15.04%. After all the headwinds, 
regulation, and badminton birds, the bottom line did what it always does – It turned up on time. 
The first rule of compounding is to never interrupt it unnecessarily. We have now delivered 36

Sanket Agrawal:

war started in Q4 FY '26, we expected tightening of liquidity and also sensed the reversal of 
interest rate environment. To this effect, we decided to keep more liquidity in our book – One, 
to ensure that no external shock derails our growth plan; and two, it gives a good cushion to 
negotiate with the lenders. Towards the end of Q1, as the market opened up from the war, we 
borrowed more than INR 2,000 crores and strengthened our borrowings with closing liquidity 
of INR 1,864 crores. This quarter, we have continued to carry the excess liquidity with closing 
number of INR 1,782 crores. The average daily borrowings were close to INR 600 crores in Q1 
and more towards INR 2,000 crores in Q2. Our LCR is at 194%. So that's on the liquidity part.  
In terms of cost of funds, our borrowing cost is 8.41% for the quarter, which is 55 bps down Y-
o-Y and 1 bp down Q-o-Q. Now as we stand with repo increase of 25 bps, we will see some 
repricing of our book, which has a mix of benchmark it is linked to. We have half of our book 
linked to MCLR, close to 20% linked to repo rate with other portion being T-Bill and other 
external benchmarks with a small portion of fixed rate loan as well. 
 
On the asset side, we have largely a variable book on MSME loans, and therefore, we will be 
able to protect the P&L from the repricing of borrowing book. We therefore, do not see a material 
compression of spreads for the reason of rate increase in the environment currently. Our yields 
are at 18%, which is currently above our guided range of 17.5%. Our spreads are at 9.63%, again, 
currently above our guided range of around 9% to 9.25%. 
 
Moving on to the business. Our AUM for September is at INR 12,592 crores with a growth of 
27% Y-o-Y and 6% on a Q-o-Q basis, with 100% of our book being secured. Our MSME AUM 
is at INR 9,669 crores, which is 77% of our AUM with a growth of 18% on a Y-o-Y basis and 
4.3% on a Q-o-Q basis. Our MSME disbursement for the quarter stands at INR 855 crores with 
a growth of 6% on a Q-o-Q basis. We've seen good momentum since December 2025, wherein 
we did INR 699 crores, then moved to INR 785 crores, which further increased to INR 809 
crores in Q1 and INR 855 crores now. We may see some increase in ticket size considering we 
have not been doing the below INR 7 lakh ticket segment.  
The loan against gold AUM is at INR 2,906 crores. We upfronted the branch expansion in H2 
of FY '26 and therefore, we have only added 1 branch during the quarter and 6 branches in the 
half year, bringing the total branch count to 257 as on September 2026.  
In terms of our cost, the Opex was slightly elevated in Q1 due to the branches opened in Q4 
2026 and the increments that were rolled out. As operating leverage kicks in, we are now 22 bps 
lower Q-o-Q at 4.07%, and we'll continue to see this reduction over the next 2 quarters.

Our GNPA is at 2.64%, which has reduced by 13 basis points Y-o-Y and 2 basis points Q-o-Q. 
We have a PCR of 42.24%, consistently above 40% over the last 2 to 3 years. Our credit cost 
for the quarter is 1.37%, which is 8 bps lower than the last quarter. It seems that the last quarter 
was the peak of credit cost unless we see a significant impact of El Nino impacting in the 
immediate future. We do not currently see signs of it affecting the portfolio, but we continue to 
remain watchful even at a regional level. It is worth noting that now our balance sheet 
provisioning is 2% of our loan assets.  
In terms of return ratios, our return on average AUM is 4.58% with ROE at 15.04% for the 
quarter. We have been conservative all through our journey when it comes to P&L. We never 
upfronted income from co-origination or similar transactions. We have kept PCR double of what 
the segment requires. We provide 2.3x of what the regulatory IRACP norms require. We now 
also carry excess liquidity in balance sheet, which has its own cost of carry and despite all this, 
we have reached an ROE of more than 15% with debt equity only at 2.31x. The idea has always 
been that can we upfront the mitigation of all the risks we can see, project it, provide for it, and 
yet make the returns. From here on, we can see expansion in our return metrics considering a 
long runway of growth before we need to raise further capital. Our PAT for the quarter is INR 
139 crores, growing 27% on a Y-o-Y basis and 7% on a Q-o-Q basis. 
 
In terms of our capital position, our capital adequacy ratio is sufficient at 31% with tangible net 
worth of INR 3,789 crores as of September 2026. We should be good till at least an AUM of 
INR 20,000 crores before we need to raise further capital. So summarizing the P&L for the 
quarter – yields are up, cost of fund is slightly down, Opex have reduced, credit costs have 
reduced, and ROEs have improved. 
 
Despite the tough environment, we have revision in outlook of our ratings by CARE and India 
Ratings from stable to positive. With scale in our sight, robust unit economics model, 
conservative provisioning policy, and a well-diversified liability franchise, we continue to move 
forward in our journey of predictable compounding.
